title: Introduction to cellular transformation and cancer genetics
why: The lecturer introduces the session, recaps histology practical observations, and outlines the learning outcomes.

title: From cell and germ theories to tumor virology
why: The lecturer traces the historical development from cell and germ theories to Rous sarcoma virus and the discovery of oncogenic viruses.

title: Retroviral capture of cellular proto-oncogenes
why: The lecturer explains how retroviruses capture cellular proto-oncogenes and how experimental transformation assays are performed.

title: Experimental assays of cellular transformation and cancer mutations
why: It explains the laboratory assays and phenotypic markers used in cell culture and animal models to test whether a gene can transform cells.

title: Functional classification of cancer genes and mutations
why: The lecturer defines oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, driver versus passenger mutations, and gatekeepers versus caretakers.

title: G1–S checkpoint regulation and its disruption in cancer
why: The lecturer explains how Rb, cyclins, CDKs, and kinase inhibitors govern the G1 to S transition and how mutations disrupt this checkpoint.

title: Mutation dominance and dominant-negative effects in p53
why: The lecturer explains how point mutations in multimeric proteins like p53 exert a dominant negative effect compared to null mutations.

title: Sequence instability and chromosomal instability in cancer
why: The lecturer defines genetic instability in cancer and contrasts chromosomal instability with sequence-level instability using karyotypes.

title: Excision repair and single-strand break repair
why: The lecturer explains mismatch repair failure leading to microsatellite instability and homologous recombination defects leading to chromosomal aberrations.

title: Mismatch repair defects and microsatellite instability
why: It examines the mismatch repair pathway, replication slippage at microsatellites, and how mutations in this pathway drive colorectal cancer.

title: Double-strand break repair defects and chromosomal instability
why: It details double-strand break repair through homologous recombination versus error-prone joining mechanisms, and how BRCA mutations cause chromosomal instability.

title: DNA polymerase epsilon mutations and sequence instability
why: The lecturer discusses polymerase epsilon mutations, lagging chromosomes in mitosis, micronuclei, chromothripsis, and the cGAS-STING stress cascade.

title: Mitotic errors and their consequences for tumor adaptation
why: The lecturer moves from DNA replication errors causing sequence instability to examining how mitotic failure produces chromosomal instability and downstream cellular consequences.

title: Mutation order and genetic instability in colorectal cancer progression
why: The lecturer presents the multistep model of tumor progression, the early role of genomic instability, and the order of mutation acquisition.

title: Hereditary cancer predisposition and tumor suppressor mutations
why: The lecturer explains Knudson's two-hit concept and examines hereditary syndromes including FAP, Lynch syndrome, BRCA-related breast cancer, and retinoblastoma.

title: BRCA2 restoration during treatment shows genetic instability is not required for malignancy
why: The lecturer explains how tumor evolution under cisplatin can restore BRCA2 function to show that genetic instability is dispensable for sustaining malignancy.

title: Lecture close: further reading and questions
why: The lecturer closes the session with recommended reading and outlines the topic for the next lecture.
